prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, bringing optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level of precision

statement.case_for: After reading all eight opening ballots I move B012 from fourth place to the front of my list. It has the strongest cross-field support (three first places, five top-three rankings, six of eight members ranking it), and the reasons are ones I recognise as an instrument builder. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice is a clean, original technique, and Ye's group turned it into the most accurate and stable clocks ever made. Systematic uncertainty has been reduced to about 1e-18, and JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and NPL reproduce and compare such clocks. That is the independent confirmation I always ask for. The consequences are concrete: tests of fundamental constants and relativity, relativistic geodesy, dark-matter searches, and a likely redefinition of the second. The attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist, with a two-person split on which all six members who ranked it proposed the same names. I have not changed my view that IceCube is a major discovery, but its support on the committee is thin and its credit problem is real (see below), so I do not think I should push it as the lead.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty and overlap. Hall and Haensch (2005, frequency combs) and Wineland and Haroche (2012, control of single quantum systems, including ion clocks) are close neighbours, and a third metrology prize in the same line could look like an incremental extension. Katori and Ye also stand on that earlier work, and Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and others have claims that two names cannot cover. The redefinition of the second has not happened, so a skeptic can say that the practical payoff is still pending. Finally, it is outside my own field, and I rely on Eva Lindroth, Stefan Kroll and Eva Olsson for the priority details.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock first as the clearest new measurement technique, with strong multi-laboratory confirmation at 1e-18, but flags possible overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I agree with his reading of the evidence, and the cross-laboratory comparisons are what convince me that systematics are under control. On overlap I am less worried than the caveat suggests. The 2005 prize rewarded the comb and the 2012 prize rewarded control of individual ions and photons. Neither rewarded the idea that removes Doppler and recoil shifts from thousands of neutral atoms at once, and that is what delivered the order-of-magnitude gain. I would still ask the committee to write the citation around the lattice concept and its realisation, not around clocks in general, so that the overlap argument does not make the prize appear to duplicate 2012.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first as a prediction followed by clear clues from nature. He ranks IceCube only seventh because the sources of the diffuse flux are unidentified, recognition may be early, and a single credited name is unfair to a large collaboration.
responses.response: On IceCube he has convinced me in part. The detection of the diffuse flux is firm, but a single-name prize for a collaboration of hundreds is hard to defend under the statutes, and the unresolved source question does make it feel early. I therefore no longer lead with B035, although I would keep it as an alternative. On twisted bilayer graphene I agree with the theory-plus-experiment pairing and with the weight of the field. I disagree on how settled it is. Several colleagues, and Olsson, Lindroth and Mehlig in their own words, note that the superconducting mechanism and twist-angle disorder are still debated, and Cao's role as first author is outside the credited names. I would accept B042 as an alternative, but I do not see it as the more mature of the two.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the optical lattice clock first as precision atomic physics: the magic-wavelength concept is Katori's, Ye drove record stability and the link to frequency combs, and the field is mature. She also notes that the 2005 and 2012 prizes might reduce perceived novelty.
responses.response: Her attribution argument is the one I rely on. Since I am not an atomic physicist, her statement that the lattice concept is clearly Katori's and the accuracy and stability record is Ye's tells me the two-name configuration is not an artefact of the supplied list. Her view that credit separation from the earlier prizes is manageable also matches mine. I would ask her to say whether Ye's contributions to the strontium clock and the many-body clock are central enough for the citation. If there is a real dispute with Lemonde's group, I want to hear it before we settle.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first and trapped ions second as foundational quantum-computing platforms, while noting that a second superconducting-circuit prize after 2025 may be unbalanced and that he should be cautious about his own proximity.
responses.response: I respect that caution, and I share the timing worry on B005, since the 2025 prize for circuit tunnelling is only a year old. Quantum computing is also a large, fast-moving area where I cannot judge decisive contributions and rely on him. But I do not think the quantum-information candidates are mature in the sense I care about. Cirac and Zoller are shared across three candidates, and Wineland's 2012 prize already covers much of the experimental credit for B020. The lattice clock does not have that problem. I would like to hear which quantum-information candidate he thinks has the fewest credit overlaps.

uncertainties: Whether the committee sees the optical lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes.
Whether Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow or other early lattice-clock groups have priority claims strong enough to disturb a Katori and Ye pairing; I am relying on atomic-physics colleagues.
Whether IceCube could be recognised fairly with one name or would need leadership beyond Halzen that the supplied list does not give.
My recollection of the history of IceCube and GRB afterglow results is from memory and unverified.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B012. My PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaboration membership and my gamma-ray polarimetry plans put me in the same field as B035 (IceCube) and B016 (GRB afterglows), so as Chair I would consider stepping back from the final decision on those two if either became the leading candidate.
